title: Q5–6: om, and the person of sixteen parts (5–6)
hook: the last two students ask about om and about a person made of sixteen parts, and one of them admits he once had to say, I don't know
carry: the sixteen parts return to the sea

segments.voice: Yesterday: the fourth question, and your line, the one who sees. Did you say goodnight to the one who sees? Today, the last two questions, and the end of the Prashna. Day four hundred ten.

Sukesha, the sixth student, opens with a story against himself. A prince of Kosala once came to me, he says, and asked: do you know the person of sixteen parts? I said, I don't know. If I knew, why wouldn't I tell you? And then he added something you don't often hear from a student: whoever speaks what isn't true dries up to the root. So I can't speak falsely. The prince got into his chariot without a word, and left. Now, Sukesha says to Pippalada, I'm asking you. Where is that person?
screen: `DO YOU KNOW THE SIXTEEN PARTS?` → `I DON'T KNOW.` → `A LIE DRIES UP TO THE ROOT.`

segments.voice: First, the fifth question, from Satyakama. What does a person win who meditates on om until the end of life? Pippalada says om is both the higher and the lower Brahman, and its sounds open different worlds. Meditate on one of its three sounds, and you come quickly back to the human world. On two, and you go to the world of the moon, and return. But one who meditates on all three, the whole of om, he says, is freed from wrong the way a snake slips out of its old skin. Then Sukesha's question. Where is the person of sixteen parts? Right here, Pippalada says, inside the body. And he tells how the sixteen arise. The self thought: when I leave, who will leave with me? It made breath. From breath, faith. Then space, wind, light, water, earth, the senses, mind and food. From food, strength. Then discipline, sacred verses, action, the worlds, and finally, name. Sixteen. Everything a life is made of. Then an image. As rivers flowing toward the sea reach it and disappear, their names and shapes broken up, and people simply say, the sea, so these sixteen parts, flowing toward the person, reach it and disappear. Their names are gone. People simply say, the person. And that one is without parts, and deathless. The six students, the text says, honored Pippalada and said: you are our father, who carries us across our ignorance to the farther shore. Six questions began with a teacher saying, if we know. They end with students saying, thank you.
screen: `OM: THE HIGHER AND THE LOWER.` · `LIKE A SNAKE OUT OF ITS SKIN.` · `SIXTEEN PARTS, FROM BREATH TO NAME.` · `RIVERS REACH THE SEA AND LOSE THEIR NAMES.` · then, large: `THE PERSON WITHOUT PARTS.`

segments.voice: Two minutes with the list of sixteen. It starts with breath and ends with name. Sit, and begin where the list begins: one breath in, one breath out. Then let a few of the others pass through your attention, in no hurry: faith, the space around you, the warmth of the body, the food you ate today, the work of your hands. Last of all, your name. Don't hold on to any of it. Then come back to the first one, the breath, and stay there. The bell holds the time.
Q5 and 6, the last two questions. Om opens the higher and lower worlds; the person of sixteen parts is right here, and the parts return to it like rivers to the sea.
screen: `Q5–6: OM AND THE SIXTEEN PARTS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the sixteen parts return to the sea. Today, if you don't know something, try Sukesha's honesty: say I don't know, plainly, and let it be enough. Day four hundred ten.

howItsDone: Om is commonly chanted at the start and close of Hindu prayer and study, and some teachers use the Prashna's line about a lie drying a person up to the root when they speak about truthfulness.

match.prompt: the last two questions — tap the pairs.

myth: Sukesha pretended to know the answer to impress the prince
he said, I don't know: a lie dries a person up to the root.
the text says the person of sixteen parts is right here, in the body
Pippalada: right here, within, is that person.
the students end by calling Pippalada their father
who carries them across ignorance to the farther shore.

fork.setup: you're Sukesha. a prince asks you a question you can't answer. what do you say?
options: make something up; he'll never check.
I don't know. if I knew, I'd tell you.
that's a secret I can't share.
fork.reveal: Sukesha said plainly, I don't know, because whoever speaks untruth dries up to the root. the prince left in silence.

original.note: Sanskrit ṣoḍaśa-kala, of sixteen parts: the person Sukesha asks about in Prashna 6.

trapdoor: what you thought: you're made of a body and maybe a soul.
what it means: the Prashna names sixteen parts, from breath to name, that return to the person like rivers to the sea.
what a scholar hears: samūlo vā eṣa pariśuṣyati yo 'nṛtam abhivadati, 'one who speaks untruth dries up to the root' (6.1); the rivers image returns in the Mundaka (3.2.8).

sources.ref: Prashna Upanishad 5.1–5.7 (om; the snake and its skin)
Prashna Upanishad 6.1–6.8 (Sukesha's confession; the sixteen parts; rivers to the sea; the students' thanks)

notes: Prashna 5: the measures of om (one, two, three) and their worlds simplified to 'one part... two parts... the whole of om'; the text speaks of three matras and the Brahma-world. Confirm the simplification is fair.
The sixteen (6.4) given from memory: prana, shraddha, kha, vayu, jyotis, apah, prthivi, indriya, manas, annam, viryam, tapas, mantrah, karma, lokah, nama. Confirm.
Hiranyanabha of Kosala is the prince; not named in the script.
Rivers image here anticipates Mundaka 3.2.8 on day 420, which will refer back.

Editor review 2026-10-01: om's measures now follow 5.3–5.5 (one, two, all three sounds); cut 'the image the whole Upanishad has been waiting for'; replaced the rivers-to-the-sea practice, which day 420 repeats almost exactly, with a practice on the list of sixteen; softened howItsDone.
